business_problem: Mapping used to be a manual process, with teams walking the peatlands and plotting features. This was immensely time-consuming and precluded any kind of national mapping because of the sheer volume of work involved.
solution_summary: Mapping used to be a manual process, with teams walking the peatlands and plotting features. This was immensely time-consuming and precluded any kind of national mapping because of the sheer volume of work involved. Natural England sought a solution to the time-consuming work of mapping damage to England's peatlands in order to focus restoration work. Working on Defra's Data Analytics and Science Hub (DASH) platform, built on Microsoft Azure and Azure Databricks, the team developed AI models to map damage to England's peat. New models and ways of working have been developed to map peatland damage and direct resources. Best practices and reusable resources can be shared across other projects and departments. What's more, as in all ecosystems, peatland plants take CO 2 from the atmosphere. However, unlike most other ecosystems, this CO isn't fully released as peatland plants decompose.

solution_components.name: Azure Databricks
solution_components.role: Processes and transforms large datasets for analytics, modeling, and downstream reporting.

data_flow: Operational and business data is gathered from the customer's source systems processed in Azure Databricks.
business_outcome: The UK's peatlands cover 12% of the country, locking in an estimated 3.2 billion tonnes of carbon. As well as being an important carbon sink, when in a natural, healthy condition

As a result, a new peat strategy is an important part of Defra's 25-year environment plan. This includes funding for peatland restoration in England.
In 2021, a proposal was put forward to use AI to map damage to English peatlands as part of the UK Civil Service Data Challenge, an initiative to promote better use of data across government.
